title: Πλούσιος καὶ θρηνῳδοί
titleEn: The Rich Man and the Mourning-Women
part: The Rich Man and the Mourning-Women (Chambry 310)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 310. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Πλούσιος δύο θυγατέρας ἔχων, τῆς ἑτέρας ἀποθανούσης, τὰς θρηνούσας ἐμισθώσατο.
sentences.tr: Plousios dyo thygateras echōn, tēs heteras apothanousēs, tas thrēnousas emisthōsato.
sentences.l: A rich man having two daughters, the one of them having died, hired the women who lament.
sentences.i: A rich man had two daughters, and when one of them died he hired the women who sing the dirge.
sentences.n: τὰς θρηνούσας with the article names a recognised trade rather than particular women: professional mourners were hired to keen at a funeral, and the title's θρηνῳδοί, 'dirge-singers', is the noun for them. ἐμισθώσατο is middle, 'hired for himself'; the active would mean letting out for hire. ἡ ἑτέρα is 'one of the two'.

sentences.t: Τῆς δὲ ἑτέρας παιδὸς λεγούσης πρὸς τὴν μητέρα· « Ἄθλιαι ἡμεῖς, εἴγε αὐταί, ὧν ἐστι τὸ πάθος, θρηνεῖν οὐκ ἴσμεν, αἱ δὲ μηδὲν προσήκουσαι οὕτω σφόδρα κόπτονται καὶ κλαίουσιν, » ἐκείνη ὑποτυχοῦσα εἶπεν· « Ἀλλὰ μὴ θαύμαζε, τέκνον, εἰ οὕτως οἰκτρῶς αὗται θρηνοῦσιν· ἐπὶ γὰρ ἀργυρίῳ τοῦτο ποιοῦσιν. »
sentences.tr: Tēs de heteras paidos legousēs pros tēn mētera· « Athliai hēmeis, eige autai, hōn esti to pathos, thrēnein ouk ismen, hai de mēden prosēkousai houtō sphodra koptontai kai klaiousin, » ekeinē hypotychousa eipen· « Alla mē thaumaze, teknon, ei houtōs oiktrōs hautai thrēnousin· epi gar argyriōi touto poiousin. »
sentences.l: And the other child saying to her mother: « Wretched are we, if indeed we ourselves, whose the suffering is, do not know how to lament, while these women, who are nothing to us, beat their breasts and weep so hard, » she, taking-up-the-word, said: « But do not wonder, child, if these women lament so piteously: for they do this for silver. »
sentences.i: And when the other daughter said to her mother: « How wretched we are, if we ourselves, whose loss it is, do not know how to lament, while these women, who are nothing to us, beat their breasts and weep so hard, » the mother answered: « Do not be surprised, child, that they lament so piteously: they do it for money. »
sentences.n: ὑποτυχοῦσα is the house verb for taking up the word in reply, not for any physical seizing. κόπτομαι in the middle is to beat one's own breast and head, the bodily half of Greek mourning, which the keeners were paid to perform. θαυμάζω εἰ, 'wonder if', is the ordinary Greek for 'be surprised that'. ὧν ἐστι τὸ πάθος is a relative in the genitive of possession, 'whose the suffering is'. ἐπί with the dative names the terms on which a thing is done: for pay.

sentences.t: Οὕτως ἔνιοι τῶν ἀνθρώπων διὰ φιλαργυρίαν οὐκ ὀκνοῦσι καὶ ἀλλοτρίας συμφορὰς ἐργολαβεῖν.
sentences.tr: Houtōs enioi tōn anthrōpōn dia philargyrian ouk oknousi kai allotrias symphoras ergolabein.
sentences.l: Thus some among men, through love of money, do not shrink from taking on even other people's misfortunes as a contract.
sentences.i: Thus some men, out of love of money, do not shrink from making a paid business even of other people's griefs.
sentences.n: ἐργολαβέω is to take a piece of work on contract — a commercial word, and the sting of the moral: grief becomes a job put out to tender. καί is 'even'. The closing formula Οὕτως ἔνιοι τῶν ἀνθρώπων … recurs across the collection, as at fables 95, 174, 176 and 204.
